problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives two to eight million personal-data documents daily, classifies them into 60 claim types with an approved EU-region LLM, and serves claims handling, fraud investigation, and analytics. Storm season brings four times the usual load.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

points.description: Scheduled parallel batches invoke the approved EU LLM for every document and publish results to a shared database with threshold review and daily metrics.
Autoscaled event workers invoke the approved EU LLM per document and publish independently consumable team events with per-type metrics.

approaches.idea: What if predictable scheduled batches handle peak volume while the approved LLM classifies every item?
What if autoscaled event workers provide elastic throughput and independent team delivery?
What if a cheap first stage protects the annual cost target and the LLM handles ambiguous cases?
What if publication waits for humans to resolve uncertainty, prioritizing review correctness?
What if human review gates publication while scheduled work and drift alerts structure the review queue?

trajectory.hypothesis: Batch capacity can meet Q1 if provisioned for the seasonal peak; full LLM inference meets R1 but threatens Q3. Shared storage delivers R2, though it weakens Q4.
trajectory.observation: Full inference gives consistent confidence and supports review, but multiplying LLM calls by peak volume makes the annual cost target doubtful; shared storage couples consumers.

trajectory.hypothesis: Elastic workers should meet Q1 and independent topics meet Q4; full LLM inference may exceed Q3.
trajectory.observation: Elastic capacity and topic fanout fit the workload and consumers; per-type counts help diagnose change but do not directly detect quality drops, and full LLM volume strains cost.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
trajectory.hypothesis: The cascade reduces average LLM calls for Q3 while preserving an LLM path for all uncertain cases; peak batch sizing is needed for Q1.
trajectory.observation: The cascade can lower cost and route uncertain work to the approved LLM and reviewers, but classifier quality, cost, and batch completion time depend on measured routing rates and capacity.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
Review: Human review before low-confidence publication
trajectory.hypothesis: Elastic execution and cheap-first inference address Q1 and Q3; holding low-confidence results for review prioritizes correctness but can delay R2.
trajectory.observation: The approach preserves uncertainty for reviewers, but review queue capacity can break the two-hour delivery expectation; quality and cost remain dependent on calibration and volumes.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing shared storage with team topics and aggregate metrics with per-type metrics should improve Q4 and Q2 without changing batch inference.
trajectory.observation: Topic fanout removes the consumer coupling, but batch sizing still needs peak validation and full inference still conflicts with cost.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
trajectory.hypothesis: Switching to the cheap-first cascade should lower cost while preserving fallback confidence; elastic capacity and team topics remain.
trajectory.observation: Cost improves in principle and autoscaling avoids fixed peak provisioning, while classifier calibration and per-type quality signals still need validation.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
trajectory.hypothesis: Claim-type drift alerts should surface quality changes within the Q2 window more directly than aggregate metrics.
trajectory.observation: Drift alerts improve signal specificity but require labeled outcomes or reliable proxies; the two-hour batch and cascade cost assumptions remain unproven.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback

Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing event workers with scheduled batches may provide orderly review workloads while retaining claim-type alerts, though it risks responsiveness.
trajectory.observation: Batching may smooth reviewer demand but can add arrival delay; holding uncertain results still puts the service target at risk.

values: Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
trajectory.hypothesis: Elastic workers address the main batch risk and drift alerts sharpen Q2; full inference remains a Q3 tradeoff.
trajectory.observation: Elasticity resolves the main throughput weakness, but full LLM inference remains a likely cost miss and drift detection needs labeled feedback.

trajectory.hypothesis: Returning to full LLM inference trades cascade calibration risk for consistent classification, while retaining autoscaling and topic benefits.
trajectory.observation: Full LLM routing simplifies confidence behavior but drops the cost benefit; metrics alone cannot assure quality-drop detection.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
trajectory.hypothesis: Autoscaling instead of scheduled batches should improve the two-hour peak target while retaining cascade economics and drift alerts.
trajectory.observation: Elasticity addresses peak arrival variation; classification quality and cost targets remain empirical, with confidence-based review avoiding a mandatory publication hold.

values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
Review: Human review before low-confidence publication
Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
trajectory.hypothesis: Autoscaling should remove the scheduled-batch latency risk while preserving review gating and the cascade's potential cost reduction.
trajectory.observation: Autoscaling cannot remove time spent waiting for human review; this option keeps the strongest review gate but still risks timely complete delivery.

adrs.title: How should classification work scale through seasonal peaks?
adrs.context: The service must complete eight million daily classifications within two hours during storm season. Scheduled parallelism offers predictable capacity planning; event-driven workers can scale with arrival variation. Neither pattern proves the target without capacity and latency measurements.

options.name: Scheduled parallel batches
pros: Predictable batch sizing and operational windows.
cons: Arrival and batch waits consume the two-hour allowance.
options.reason: Chosen where forecastable batch capacity is acceptable.

options.name: Event-driven autoscaling
pros: Elastic response to variable and seasonal arrivals.
cons: Scaling limits and downstream LLM capacity still need validation.
options.reason: Preferred for peak elasticity, though review latency can remain.

adrs.title: How should the LLM be used within the cost target?
adrs.context: Every document needs a claim type and confidence, annual average classification cost must stay below the stated limit, and inference must use the approved provider in its EU region. Full LLM inference is simple but expensive at millions of items; a first-stage classifier can save calls but needs validated quality and calibrated fallback.

options.name: LLM for every document
pros: Consistent use of the approved model and confidence source.
cons: Likely exceeds the cost target at this volume.
options.reason: Retained as a quality-forward comparison despite cost risk.

options.name: Cheap-first cascade with approved LLM fallback
values: Inference: Cheap-first cascade with LLM fallback
pros: Can reduce average expensive model calls.
cons: Accuracy, confidence calibration, and cost depend on routing rates and first-stage quality.
options.reason: Preferred for cost-aware alternatives, pending measured validation.

adrs.title: How should uncertain results and corrections flow?
adrs.context: Three teams need results, low-confidence documents need human review, and corrections should improve classification. Independent delivery contracts limit coordination; holding uncertain outputs for review can improve their quality but adds queue latency.

options.name: Threshold review with team topics
pros: Uncertain cases enter a correction loop while consumers process independent streams.
cons: Results may be provisional before correction; review feedback integration must be built.
options.reason: Balances timely delivery with reviewer feedback and consumer autonomy.

options.name: Review-gated team topics
values: Review: Human review before low-confidence publication
pros: Low-confidence results are corrected before consumers see them.
cons: Human queue delays can violate the delivery window.
options.reason: Kept as a correctness-oriented alternative with explicit latency risk.

adrs.title: How should localized quality loss become visible?
adrs.context: Operators need to see degradation for an individual claim type within a day. Aggregate daily metrics can miss localized changes; type metrics help isolate issues, while drift alerts can be more direct but need a signal tied to labeled outcomes or reliable proxies.

options.name: Per-claim-type metrics
cons: Metrics do not themselves detect quality loss.
options.reason: Included as a baseline monitoring choice.

options.name: Drift alerts by claim type
values: Monitoring: Drift alerts by claim type
pros: Targets localized distribution or quality changes.
cons: Alert validity and timeliness depend on suitable signals and labeled outcomes.
options.reason: Preferred for the one-day detection objective, with signal design still required.

options.name: Aggregate daily metrics
cons: Can hide degradation isolated to one claim type.
options.reason: Set aside because the required signal is localized by claim type.

adrs.title: Where must documents and model calls be processed?
adrs.context: Personal data must remain in the EU, and the approved provider must serve inference from its EU region. Processing placement constrains storage, workers, and model calls across every alternative.

options.name: EU region processing
pros: Keeps data processing and approved model calls in the permitted region.
cons: Logs, backups, queues, and review tooling also need in-region operation.
options.reason: Every alternative keeps document processing in the insurer EU region.
